title: The Drifting Carriages
author: Nell Ardwick
variants:
I have crossed
eleven hundred
carriages.

Nine were made
by hands.


You know one because
it is finished.

The train scatters. It
leaves a chest sunk
half into a wall, a
stair going nowhere,
a lantern hung where
no-one stands.

A drifting carriage
has none of that.
Every block was set
on purpose, by
someone who meant it.


The others gave them
the name.

I did not.
I only started counting.

A man in the copper
cars taught me
to wait.


You step in and the
room says something
about itself.

Then nothing.

Most of us walk on
through the nothing.
He never did.


Stand still, he said.
Count three, slowly.

The names come then.
Late and quiet, like
someone remembering
they ought to say.


They come either way.

But if you don't wait,
you are already through
the far door, and the
names arrive behind you,
for no-one.

The ninth was mine.


I made it in the mud
carriages, a long
way back.

A bench. A table.
A chest I filled
and left.

Then it was gone,
the way rooms go.


It came back to me
four hundred
carriages later.

The bench was where
I put it.

The table was not.


Someone had turned it
to face the window.

Someone after them
had set flowers on it.

The names came.
None of them
were mine.

Not all of them
were made.

One was waiting
to be.


Walls, floor, a door
at either end, and
nothing in it that
anybody chose.

It is not empty the
way a looted room
is empty.

It is empty the way
a page is.


The man who showed it
to me would not
touch it.

The first thing you
set down decides what
the room becomes, he
said, and he did not
trust himself
to decide.


I went back for it.
It was gone.

Someone less careful
than him has it now.

One day I will walk
into what they chose.

The chests in them are
not the train's chests.


A train chest is a
handful of things
thrown together.
Bread, a bent sword,
nine arrows.

A made room's chest is
what one person chose
to leave you.


I opened one that held
nothing but bread.

Twelve loaves,
stacked even.

Somebody went hungry
to do that.


I took six.
I left six.

I have never been able
to explain to anyone
why that felt like the
sum I was asked for.

They come back where
they were made.


I have never found a
room in the sand that
somebody built in
the dark.

Never a mud room
in the copper cars.

Not once.


Whatever carries them
knows where they
came from.

It will take a room
a very long way.

It will not take it
out of its own country.
